verses.zh: 巴兰对巴勒说：「你在这里给我筑七座坛，为我预备七只公牛，七只公羊。」
verses.en: [NOTE:1] Balaam said to Balak, “Build me seven altars here, and prepare for me here seven bulls and seven rams.”
notes: The first part of Balaam’s activity ends in disaster for Balak—he blesses Israel. The chapter falls into four units: the first prophecy (vv. 1-10), the relocation (vv. 11-17), the second prophecy (vv. 18-24), and a further location (vv. 25-30).

verses.zh: 巴勒照巴兰的话行了。巴勒和巴兰在每座坛上献一只公牛，一只公羊。
verses.en: So Balak did just as Balaam had said. Balak and Balaam then offered on each[NOTE:1] altar a bull and a ram.
notes: The Hebrew text has “on the altar,” but since there were seven of each animal and seven altars, the implication is that this means on each altar.

verses.zh: 巴兰对巴勒说：「你站在你的燔祭旁边，我且往前去，或者耶和华来迎见我。他指示我甚么，我必告诉你。」于是巴兰上一净光的高处。
verses.en: Balaam said to Balak, “Station yourself[NOTE:1] by your burnt offering, and I will go off; perhaps the Lord will come to meet me, and whatever he reveals to me[NOTE:2] I will tell you.”[NOTE:3] Then he went to a deserted height.[NOTE:4]
notes: The verb הִתְיַצֵּב (hityatsev) means “to take a stand, station oneself.” It is more intentional than simply standing by something. He was to position himself by the sacrifice as Balaam withdrew to seek the oracle.

Heb “and the word of what he shows me.” The noun is in construct, and so the clause that follows functions as a noun clause in the genitive. The point is that the word will consist of divine revelation.
The verb is the perfect tense with vav (ו) consecutive. This clause is dependent on the clause that precedes it.
He went up to a bald spot, to a barren height. The statement underscores the general belief that such tops were the closest things to the gods. On such heights people built their shrines and temples.

verses.zh: 神迎见巴兰；巴兰说：「我预备了七座坛，在每座坛上献了一只公牛，一只公羊。」
verses.en: Then God met Balaam, who[NOTE:1] said to him, “I have prepared seven altars, and I have offered on each altar a bull and a ram.”
notes: The relative pronoun is added here in place of the conjunction to clarify that Balaam is speaking to God and not vice versa.

verses.zh: 耶和华将话传给巴兰，又说：「你回到巴勒那里，要如此如此说。」
verses.en: Then the Lord put a message[NOTE:1] in Balaam’s mouth and said, “Return to Balak, and speak what I tell you.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “word.”
Heb “and thus you shall speak.”

verses.zh: 他就回到巴勒那里，见他同摩押的使臣都站在燔祭旁边。
verses.en: So he returned to him, and he was still[NOTE:1] standing by his burnt offering, he and all the princes of Moab.
notes: The Hebrew text draws the vividness of the scene with the deictic particle הִנֵּה (hinneh)—Balaam returned, and there he was, standing there.

verses.zh: 巴兰便题起诗歌说：巴勒引我出亚兰，摩押王引我出东山，说：来啊，为我咒诅雅各；来啊，怒骂以色列。
verses.en: Then Balaam[NOTE:1] uttered[NOTE:2] his oracle, saying, “Balak, the king of Moab, brought me[NOTE:3] from Aram, out of the mountains of the east, saying, ‘Come, pronounce a curse on Jacob for me; come, denounce Israel.’[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (Balaam) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “took up.”

The passage calls for a past tense translation; since the verb form is a prefixed conjugation, this tense should be classified as a preterite without the vav (ו). Such forms do occur, especially in the ancient poetic passages.

The opening lines seem to be a formula for the seer to identify himself and the occasion for the oracle. The tension is laid out early; Balaam knows that God has intended to bless Israel, but he has been paid to curse them.

verses.zh: 神没有咒诅的，我焉能咒诅？耶和华没有怒骂的，我焉能怒骂？
verses.en: How[NOTE:1] can I curse[NOTE:2] one whom God has not cursed, or how can I denounce one whom the Lord has not denounced?
notes: The figure is erotesis, a rhetorical question. He is actually saying he cannot curse them because God has not cursed them.
The imperfect tense should here be classified as a potential imperfect.

verses.zh: 我从高峰看他，从小山望他；这是独居的民，不列在万民中。
verses.en: For from the top of the rocks I see them;[NOTE:1] from the hills I watch them.[NOTE:2] Indeed, a nation that lives alone, and it will not be reckoned[NOTE:3] among the nations.
notes: Heb “him,” but here it refers to the Israelites (Israel).

Balaam reports his observation of the nation of Israel spread out below him in the valley. Based on that vision, and the Lord’s word, he announces the uniqueness of Israel—they are not just like one of the other nations. He was correct, of course; they were the only people linked with the living God by covenant.
The verb could also be taken as a reflexive—Israel does not consider itself as among the nations, meaning, they consider themselves to be unique.

verses.zh: 谁能数点雅各的尘土？谁能计算以色列的四分之一？我愿如义人之死而死；我愿如义人之终而终。
verses.en: Who[NOTE:1] can count[NOTE:2] the dust[NOTE:3] of Jacob, or number[NOTE:4] the fourth part of Israel? Let me[NOTE:5] die the death of the upright,[NOTE:6] and let the end of my life[NOTE:7] be like theirs.”[NOTE:8]
notes: The question is again rhetorical; it means no one can count them—they are innumerable.
The perfect tense can also be classified as a potential nuance. It does not occur very often, but does occur several times.

The reference in the oracle is back to Gen 13:16, which would not be clear to Balaam. But God had described their growth like the dust of the earth. Here it is part of the description of the vast numbers.

Heb “and as a number, the fourth part of Israel.” The noun in the MT is not in the construct state, and so it should be taken as an adverbial accusative, forming a parallel with the verb “count.” The second object of the verse then follows, “the fourth part of Israel.” Smr and the LXX have “and who has numbered” (וּמִסְפָּר, umispar), making this colon more parallel to the preceding one. The editor of BHS prefers this reading.
The use of נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) for the subject of the verb stresses the personal nature—me.

Here the seer’s words link with the promise of Gen 12:3, that whoever blesses Israel will be blessed. Since the blessing belongs to them, the upright (and not Balak), Balaam would like his lot to be with them.
Heb “my latter end.”
Heb “his.”

verses.zh: 巴勒对巴兰说：「你向我做的是甚么事呢？我领你来咒诅我的仇敌，不料，你竟为他们祝福。」
verses.en: Then Balak said to Balaam, “What have you done to me? I brought you to curse my enemies, but on the contrary[NOTE:1] you have only blessed them!”[NOTE:2]
notes: The Hebrew text uses הִנֵּה (hinneh) here to stress the contrast.

The construction is emphatic, using the perfect tense and the infinitive absolute to give it the emphasis. It would have the force of “you have done nothing but bless,” or “you have indeed blessed.” The construction is reminiscent of the call of Abram and the promise of the blessing in such elaborate terms.

verses.zh: 他回答说：「耶和华传给我的话，我能不谨慎传说吗？」
verses.en: Balaam replied,[NOTE:1] “Must I not be careful[NOTE:2] to speak what the Lord has put in my mouth?”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “he answered and said.” The referent (Balaam) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The verb שָׁמַר (shamar) means “to guard, watch, observe” and so here with a sense of “be careful” or even “take heed” (so KJV, ASV). The nuance of the imperfect tense would be obligatory: “I must be careful”—to do what? to speak what the Lord has put in my mouth. The infinitive construct “to speak” is therefore serving as the direct object of שָׁמַר.
The clause is a noun clause serving as the direct object of “to speak.” It begins with the sign of the accusative, and then the relative pronoun that indicates the whole clause is the accusative.

verses.zh: 巴勒说：「求你同我往别处去，在那里可以看见他们；你不能全看见，只能看见他们边界上的人。在那里要为我咒诅他们。」
verses.en: Balak said to him, “Please come with me to another place from which you can observe them. You will see only a part of them, but you will not see all of them. Curse them for me from there.”

verses.zh: 于是领巴兰到了琐腓田，上了毗斯迦山顶，筑了七座坛；每座坛上献一只公牛，一只公羊。
verses.en: So Balak brought Balaam[NOTE:1] to the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah,[NOTE:2] where[NOTE:3] he built seven altars and offered a bull and a ram on each altar.
notes: Heb “he brought him”; the referents (Balak and Balaam) have been specified in the translation for clarity.
Some scholars do not translate this word as “Pisgah,” but rather as a “lookout post” or an “elevated place.”
Heb “and he built.”

verses.zh: 巴兰对巴勒说：「你站在这燔祭旁边，等我往那边去迎见耶和华。」
verses.en: And Balaam[NOTE:1] said to Balak, “Station yourself here[NOTE:2] by your burnt offering, while I meet the Lord there.”
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (Balaam) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The verse uses כֹּה (koh) twice: “Station yourself here…I will meet [the Lord] there.”

verses.zh: 耶和华临到巴兰那里，将话传给他；又说：「你回到巴勒那里，要如此如此说。」
verses.en: Then the Lord met Balaam and put a message[NOTE:1] in his mouth and said, “Return to Balak, and speak what I tell you.”
notes: Heb “word.”

verses.zh: 他就回到巴勒那里，见他站在燔祭旁边；摩押的使臣也和他在一处。巴勒问他说：「耶和华说了甚么话呢？」
verses.en: When Balaam[NOTE:1] came to him, he was still standing by his burnt offering, along with the princes of Moab. And Balak said to him, “What has the Lord spoken?”
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (Balaam) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 巴兰就题诗歌说：巴勒，你起来听；西拨的儿子，你听我言。
verses.en: Balaam[NOTE:1] uttered[NOTE:2] his oracle, and said,“Rise up,[NOTE:3] Balak, and hear;Listen to me, son of Zippor:
notes: Heb “he.” The antecedent has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
Heb “took up.”
The verb probably means “pay attention” in this verse.

verses.zh: 神非人，必不致说谎，也非人子，必不致后悔。他说话岂不照着行呢？他发言岂不要成就呢？
verses.en: God is not a man, that he should lie,nor a human being,[NOTE:1] that he should change his mind.Has he said, and will he not do it?Or has he spoken, and will he not make it happen?[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “son of man.”
The verb is the Hiphil of קוּם (qum, “to cause to rise; to make stand”). The meaning here is more of the sense of fulfilling the promises made.

verses.zh: 我奉命祝福；　神也曾赐福，此事我不能翻转。
verses.en: Indeed, I have received a command[NOTE:1] to bless;he has blessed,[NOTE:2] and I cannot reverse it.[NOTE:3]
notes: The Hebrew text simply has “I have received [to] bless.” The infinitive is the object of the verb, telling what he received. Balaam was not actually commanded to bless, but was given the word of blessing so that he was given a divine decree that would bless Israel.
The reference is probably to the first speech, where the Lord blessed Israel. Balaam knows that there is nothing he can do to reverse what God has said.
The verb is the Hiphil of שׁוּב (shuv), meaning “to cause to return.” He cannot return God’s word to him, for it has been given, and it will be fulfilled.

verses.zh: 他未见雅各中有罪孽，也未见以色列中有奸恶。耶和华―他的　神和他同在；有欢呼王的声音在他们中间。
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] has not looked on iniquity in Jacob,[NOTE:2] nor has he seen trouble[NOTE:3] in Israel.The Lord their God is with them;his acclamation[NOTE:4] as king is among them.
notes: These could be understood as impersonal and so rendered “no one has discovered.”

The line could mean that God has regarded Israel as the ideal congregation without any blemish or flaw. But it could also mean that God has not looked on their iniquity, meaning, held it against them.

The word means “wrong, misery, trouble.” It can mean the idea of “disaster” as well, for that too is trouble. Here it is parallel to “iniquity” and so has the connotation of something that would give God reason to curse them.

The people are blessed because God is their king. In fact, the shout of acclamation is among them—they are proclaiming the Lord God as their king. The word is used normally for the sound of the trumpet, but also of battle shouts, and then here acclamation. This would represent their conviction that Yahweh is king. On the usage of this Hebrew word see further BDB 929-30 s.v. תְּרוּעָה; HALOT 1790-91 s.v.

verses.zh: 神领他们出埃及；他们似乎有野牛之力。
verses.en: God brought them[NOTE:1] out of Egypt.They have, as it were, the strength of a wild bull.[NOTE:2]
notes: The form is the Hiphil participle from יָצַא (yatsaʾ) with the object suffix. He is the one who brought them out.
The expression is “the horns of the wild ox” (KJV “unicorn”). The point of the image is strength or power. Horns are also used in the Bible to represent kingship (see Pss 89; 132).

verses.zh: 断没有法术可以害雅各，也没有占卜可以害以色列。现在必有人论及雅各，就是论及以色列说：　神为他行了何等的大事！
verses.en: For there is no spell[NOTE:1] against[NOTE:2] Jacob,nor is there any divination against Israel.At this time[NOTE:3] it must be said[NOTE:4] of Jacoband of Israel, ‘Look at[NOTE:5] what God has done!’
notes: The words נַחַשׁ (nakhash, “magic curse, omen”) and קֶסֶם (qesem, “prediction, divination”) describe two techniques of consulting gods. The first concerns omens generally, perhaps the flight of birds (HALOT 690 s.v.). The second relates to casting lots, sometimes done with arrows (Ezek 21:26). See N. H. Snaith, Leviticus and Numbers (NCB), 295-296.
The ASV says “with Jacob,” but most translations use “against” (both are theoretically possible) because of the context, esp. v. 20.
The form is the preposition “like, as” and the word for “time”—according to the time, about this time, now.
The Niphal imperfect here carries the nuance of obligation—one has to say in amazement that God has done something marvelous or “it must be said.”
The words “look at” are not in the Hebrew text but have been added in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 这民起来，彷佛母狮，挺身，好像公狮，未曾吃野食，未曾喝被伤者之血，决不躺卧。
verses.en: Indeed, the people will rise up like a lioness,and like a lion raises himself up;they will not lie down until they eat their[NOTE:1] prey,and drink the blood of the slain.”[NOTE:2]
notes: The pronoun “their” has been supplied for clarity; it is not present in the Hebrew text.

The oracle compares Israel first to a lion, or better, lioness, because she does the tracking and hunting of food while the lion moves up and down roaring and distracting the prey. But the lion is also the traditional emblem of Judah, Dan and Gad, as well as the symbol of royalty. So this also supports the motif of royalty as well as power for Israel.

verses.zh: 巴勒对巴兰说：「你一点不要咒诅他们，也不要为他们祝福。」
verses.en: Balak said to Balaam, “Neither curse them at all[NOTE:1] nor bless them at all!”[NOTE:2]
notes: The verb is preceded by the infinitive absolute: “you shall by no means curse” or “do not curse them at all.” He brought him to curse, and when he tried to curse there was a blessing. Balak can only say it would be better not to bother.

The same construction now works with “nor bless them at all.” The two together form a merism—“don’t say anything.” He does not want them blessed, so Balaam is not to do that, but the curse isn’t working either.

verses.zh: 巴兰回答巴勒说：「我岂不是告诉你说『凡耶和华所说的，我必须遵行』吗？」
verses.en: But Balaam replied[NOTE:1] to Balak, “Did I not tell you, ‘All that the Lord speaks,[NOTE:2] I must do’?”
notes: Heb “answered and said.”

This first clause, “all that the Lord speaks”—is a noun clause functioning as the object of the verb that comes at the end of the verse. It is something of an independent accusative case, since it is picked up with the sign of the accusative: “all that the Lord speaks, it I must do.”

verses.zh: 巴勒对巴兰说：「来吧，我领你往别处去，或者　神喜欢你在那里为我咒诅他们。」
verses.en: Balak said to Balaam, “Come, please; I will take you to another place. Perhaps it will please God[NOTE:1] to let you curse them for me from there.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “be pleasing in the eyes of God.”

Balak is stubborn, as indeed Balaam is persistent. But Balak still thinks that if another location were used it just might work. Balaam had actually told Balak in the prophecy that other attempts would fail. But Balak refuses to give up so easily. So he insists they perform the ritual and try again. This time, however, Balaam will change his approach, and this will result in a dramatic outpouring of power on him.

verses.zh: 巴勒就领巴兰到那下望旷野的毗珥山顶上。
verses.en: So Balak took Balaam to the top of Peor, that looks toward the wastelands.[NOTE:1]
notes: Or perhaps as a place name, “Jeshimon” (cf. 21:20).

verses.zh: 巴兰对巴勒说：「你在这里为我筑七座坛，又在这里为我预备七只公牛，七只公羊。」
verses.en: Then Balaam said to Balak, “Build seven altars here for me, and prepare seven bulls and seven rams.”

verses.zh: 巴勒就照巴兰的话行，在每座坛上献一只公牛，一只公羊。
verses.en: So Balak did as Balaam had said, and offered a bull and a ram on each altar.
